title: Degron mutation effects at residue level
notes: This is an introduction and research progress discussion with a lecturer, rather than a final thesis defense. The opening visual uses measured HIF1A mutation labels. The aim is to explain the task, present the evidence available so far and discuss the next research steps.

title: Degrons participate in protein degradation
insight: An amino acid substitution can alter the recognition signal.
notes: The diagram is a simplified illustration of the ubiquitin–proteasome system. The Fam188a GIF by Nikolakhs, licensed CC BY-SA 3.0, illustrates a folded protein; it is not a measured HIF1A or degron structure. A peptide assayed in isolation may behave differently within the full protein.

title: One substitution corresponds to one cell in the effect map
insight: Input: WT sequence, position and replacement amino acid. Output: ΔPSI.
notes: WT is the reference sequence. The display has 28 positions and 20 amino acids; WT-to-WT cells are masked, leaving up to 532 genuine substitutions. This diagram explains the output format and does not show model predictions.

title: GPS converts reporter measurements into ΔPSI labels
insight: ΔPSI = PSI(mutant) − PSI(WT). Positive: a more stable reporter in this assay.
notes: The histogram illustrates the measurement principle rather than actual counts. The Zhang assay uses six bins and a PSI scale from 1 to 6; lower PSI indicates a less stable reporter. A positive ΔPSI means the mutant reporter is more stable than WT. The sign alone does not establish an E3 mechanism or pathogenicity.

title: HIF1A illustrates position-specific mutation effects
insight: Within one peptide, mutation effects differ substantially across positions.
notes: The example is Q16665_HIF1A_25, residues 553–580 of HIF1A. Intrinsic WT PSI is 2.1865; 529 substitutions were measured and 186 have ΔPSI ≥ 1. Selection required at least 500 measured cells, then the highest positive-cell count, with ID as the tie-breaker. The connection to the HIF1A/VHL motif is a literature cross-check, not a newly discovered mechanism. WT and missing cells are masked.

title: The practical goal is to prioritize mutations for experiments
insight: Effect map → shortlist → experimental validation.
notes: Predicted ranking helps design experiments but does not replace them. ClinVar supplies annotations and motivation; a residue-level relationship to pathogenicity has not been established. The schematic cells represent prioritization, not numerical model scores.

title: Related approaches address different questions
insight: Focus: predictive evidence, evaluation and a useful analysis tool.
notes: An effect map or a web application is not an exclusive novelty claim. AUROCs for different endpoints and prediction units cannot be directly compared. Degformer already provides mutation maps. MetaDegron uses a shared classifier with motif/E3 choices; menu entries are not separately learned E3 classes. The defensible focus is measured labels, evaluation, strong baselines and practical utility.

title: Three objectives connect research to an analysis tool
insight: Main scope: single-substitution effects in 28-residue reporter peptides.
notes: The main task is predicting single-substitution effects in 28-residue reporter peptides. E3 specificity and clinical classification are outside the primary task. No new biological measurements were collected. The tool supports hypothesis generation and experimental prioritization.

title: Questions guiding the current research
insight: Each question needs an appropriate comparison and clear limits of inference.
notes: These are related research questions, not a timeline of runs. Findings are grouped by the question addressed rather than by experiment codes or execution dates. Source transfer, representations and practical reliability each require their own comparisons.

title: Each data source serves a defined role
insight: Tile-level scores and annotations are not mutation-effect labels.
notes: The core full-range dataset contains Zhang measurements and UniProt sequence information. It does not contain ClinVar, Koren, Larsen, MetaDegron or model weights. Voutsinos supplies a tile-level transfer task and PAP baseline resources. Keep downloaded, audited and fitted sources conceptually separate.

title: The two mutation designs provide complementary coverage
insight: Scanning expands context coverage; saturation covers all substitution types.
notes: The scanning replacement is determined by the WT amino acid, with targets R, A or S. It therefore covers 20 directed substitution types out of 380 non-synonymous types. The schematic shows the design, not a claim that every cell passes QC. Saturation provides the broader substitution matrix needed for this task.

title: Each assay needs the correct WT reference
insight: Keep sources, conditions and replicates separate when deriving effect labels.
notes: Saturation has no direct mut0 reference, so the WT reference is the median of synonymous constructs within each half. Scanning uses mut0 from the correct replicate. BAG6 WT must not be used as the saturation reference. Reconstructing 261,865 published PSI values matched within 5 × 10⁻⁷ when the published processing conditions were reproduced.

title: Label reproducibility constrains how results should be interpreted
insight: Model residuals can contain both signal and measurement noise.
notes: The Pearson correlation of ΔPSI between the two saturation halves is 0.8335 on the audited cohort. Peptide-level reliability is different from position- or cell-level reproducibility. Noise as a fraction of residual variance must not be compared with noise as a fraction of total variance as though they had the same denominator. Replicates describe measurement reliability rather than a universal ceiling for every possible estimator.

title: Split by protein group to assess generalization
insight: Restricted domain: 91 peptides. Full range: 235 peptides in 221 protein groups.
notes: The restricted-domain and full-range designs differ in population, eligibility and preprocessing; their AUROCs must not be joined into a single progression curve. The full-range design uses five outer folds and three inner-validation seeds. Transformations are fitted within training data. Neural epochs are selected on inner validation before reinitialization and outer-training refit. Homology control is heuristic, not proof of complete biological independence.

title: Prediction error, ranking and experimental budget are distinct goals
insight: Compute metrics per peptide; bootstrap confidence intervals by protein group.
notes: Full-range MAE uses all 235 peptides. Positive events, measured ΔPSI ≥ 1, have 184 eligible peptides; negative events, ΔPSI ≤ −1, have 110. Both classes need at least three cells. Confidence intervals use 5,000 protein-group bootstrap resamples, not 122,412 independent mutation cells. AUROC is not accuracy, and AP must be read with event prevalence.

title: Local context adds information beyond the substitution itself
insight: A context baseline is essential before adding model complexity.
notes: On the scanning evaluation, substitution plus composition achieves AUROC 0.8393; unordered local composition reaches 0.8625; ordered local context reaches 0.8682. The paired ordered-context improvement is 0.0289, with a 95% interval from 0.0264 to 0.0313. This source reports mean seed AUROC, not the full-range prediction ensemble. A composition-only linear term cannot independently distinguish positions with the same substitution within a peptide.

title: Training across the PSI range reduces Ridge regression error
insight: Error improves, but the adjusted interval does not establish a minimum 0.02 PSI reduction.
notes: The comparison uses the same 235 test peptides and 221 protein groups. Full-range training reduces MAE by 5.94% relative to training only at PSI ≤ 4. The two primary comparisons use adjusted 97.5% confidence intervals. The bound nearest zero does not establish a minimum reduction of 0.02 PSI. Restricted training still uses full-range validation. WT PSI is metadata, not a model feature or a test-time clipping input.

title: Full-range training benefits high-PSI peptides most
insight: Choose the training distribution for both the overall objective and the intended domain.
notes: The four PSI strata contain 91, 85, 36 and 23 peptides. Balancing helps high-PSI peptides but can trade off low-PSI performance. PSI > 5 cannot have a positive event ΔPSI ≥ 1, so positive AUROC is undefined there. Ridge guardrails do not automatically transfer to CNN: compared with a CNN trained only at PSI ≤ 4, full-range CNN increases low-PSI MAE by about 0.00870, and its AUROC interval does not establish the 0.01 guardrail.

title: ESM adds signal to the context baseline
insight: Only ESM2-35M was evaluated on the full-range benchmark; pLM families cannot yet be ranked.
notes: Adding ESM to context Ridge improves positive AUROC by about 0.01255, with a descriptive 95% interval from 0.00622 to 0.01967. Validation-based nested selection reaches MAE 0.397525, but its AUROC gain remains unresolved. A fixed recipe cannot substitute for evaluation of the selection procedure. Only ESM2-35M has been evaluated on the full-range benchmark.

title: A CNN adds value after the ESM representation
insight: The matched-input comparison supports position mixing; one-hot results remain unresolved.
notes: With the same representation and full-range training, CNN reduces MAE by 0.00534 versus pointwise, with a descriptive 95% interval from −0.01017 to −0.00090. Positive AUROC increases by about 0.01129. Pointwise and CNN heads have 36,833 and 57,185 parameters, respectively, so this is not a complete isolation of position mixing from model capacity.

title: Multiple windows have not shown a clear advantage over one
insight: The best development MAE alone is insufficient to select a final model.
notes: The balanced multi-window model has MAE 0.383846 versus 0.384354 for the full-range CNN. The difference, −0.000508, has a descriptive 95% interval from −0.003157 to +0.002223; the two training distributions also differ. With the same full-range training, multiple windows likewise have no demonstrated advantage. A CNN trained only at PSI ≤ 4 remains relevant when prioritizing the low-PSI domain.

title: Learning tile scores well does not guarantee mutation-effect transfer
insight: The negative result applies to the tested transfer design, not to all pretraining strategies.
notes: The comparison uses the same encoder, fine-tuning procedure and 91-peptide evaluation domain. Pretraining on 212,616 tiles learns its own task well, with Pearson correlation around 0.864. After fine-tuning, AUROC is 0.8098 versus 0.8175 from random initialization; the difference interval still includes zero. The negative conclusion applies to this tile-label transfer design, not to all pLMs or all transfer strategies.

title: Scanning pretraining helps beyond the observed substitution types
insight: Quality weighting increases error; averaging replicates has no clear advantage over replicate 1.
notes: This is a one-hot CNN, not an ESM-plus-scanning experiment. The 20-type cohort has 6,433 cells and the remaining 360 types have 115,979 cells; both cover 235 peptides and 221 groups. Both MAE intervals favor improvement, but these are descriptive posthoc diagnostics. Averaging replicates has no clear advantage over replicate 1, and quality weighting increases MAE by about 0.00401. These are saturation OOF findings, not held-source T results.

title: Degformer comparisons require overlap and training-data audits
insight: Group-clean retraining reaches AUROC 0.8068, with no demonstrated advantage over Ridge.
notes: The published checkpoint has 42,163 of the 47,847 mutation cells and WT sequences for all 91 peptides in its training data. Removing duplicate cells does not produce a peptide holdout. Group-clean retraining reaches AUROC 0.806775 versus 0.820822 for Ridge with expanded training; the difference interval includes zero. Do not interpret the checkpoint/retraining difference as a causal effect of leakage alone because training conditions also change.

title: Ranking focuses the experimental budget on promising substitutions
insight: This demonstrates prioritization utility, not calibrated probabilities.
notes: Positive precision is macro-averaged over 184 eligible peptides. At the top 5%, CNN reaches 58.24% versus 51.89% for Ridge; at the top 10%, the values are 49.04% and 44.29%. Positive AP is 0.50947 with macro prevalence 0.124697. For negative events, AP is 0.213667 over 110 peptides and top-5% precision is about 16.77%. These are ranking utilities, not whole-dataset accuracy or calibrated probabilities.

title: Model selection also depends on stability and cost
insight: Ensembling reduces variance; seeds and folds are not independent datasets.
notes: CNN improves MAE over Ridge on 156 of 235 peptides and across all five folds. Completed task time totals 9.3265 hours, including 7.23 hours for two frozen-backbone tasks. The frozen branch has seed 17 with five folds; LoRA has no complete OOF output. A saved running status does not establish that a remote process is still alive. Do not merge results from a different local runtime into this Kaggle snapshot.

title: Calibration maps regression scores to event probabilities
insight: Calibration evidence belongs to the tested model; the CNN needs its own calibration procedure.
notes: This calibration evidence belongs to Ridge, evaluated out of fold on 91 peptides. Platt calibration has Brier score about 0.0925 versus 0.1139 for the prevalence baseline. A ΔPSI regression score is not itself a probability. Reliability remains somewhat biased low because calibration-pool and test-domain distributions differ; it is not perfect calibration. CNN needs its own calibrator and evaluation procedure.

title: Assess the applicability domain alongside predictions
insight: PSI differs across sources; a peptide model does not establish whole-protein effects.
notes: The gate was studied for the training domain PSI ≤ 4. Peptidome-screen PSI differs from intrinsic WT PSI by about 0.9, so the raw threshold 4 cannot be directly reused. In-domain, borderline and out-of-domain states describe data applicability, not guaranteed ΔPSI accuracy. Full-range training also does not establish applicability to every protein. Correct integration of the gate into the baseline app remains open.

title: The tool combines the effect map and shortlist in one workflow
insight: Enter a peptide → inspect the map → select substitutions → annotate → export.
notes: The screenshot shows the current Workspace UI v2 design prototype, cropped to the effect map and inspector. Every displayed score and probability is a synthetic fixture; there is no model inference or backend. The React/FastAPI baseline is separate code. This image illustrates the workflow and does not certify the expanded features.

title: A local application keeps results with their provenance
insight: Each result carries its model version, data sources and intended scope.
notes: The selected stack is local React/TypeScript and FastAPI. SQLite has been used for the baseline; PostgreSQL and durable workspace storage still require implementation and verification. Public hosting is not required. The diagram explains architecture and provenance rather than claiming that every module is complete.

title: The software baseline provides a foundation for extension
insight: Baseline tests retain their original scope; extensions require separate verification.
notes: The tests recorded in the documentation cover the baseline and were not rerun while building this deck. Projects/history, durable batch jobs, whole-protein web workflows and experimental-data import still require implementation under the expanded scope. The new domain gate has not been correctly integrated into the baseline. A designed endpoint is not an accepted implementation.

title: Completed work provides a foundation for the next research steps
insight: Development findings and explicit limitations now guide the next steps.
notes: Connect the available artifacts and findings back to the three initial objectives. The developing contribution includes data/benchmark construction, experimental methodology, evaluation and software. A new architecture is not required to explain the research value. This is a progress discussion rather than a claim that the thesis is complete.

title: Next priorities: lock the model choice and evaluate transfer
insight: LoRA and structure remain optional branches, guided by the question and available resources.
notes: Automatic final promotion currently supports context Ridge; CNN needs architecture-specific final refitting and export. Lock the recipe and calibration before reading T. Scanning has previously been explored, so T must be described with its held-source scope and exposure history. Model research and tool development can proceed in parallel. Completing LoRA is not a prerequisite for the core benchmark.

title: Discussion: research direction and next steps
notes: Invite feedback on research objectives and priorities: overall regression versus strong-event prioritization, the appropriate generalization test, and software scope. This is an introduction/progress meeting, not final acceptance. Use the overview and appendices when a detailed comparison is useful.

title: Terminology and how to read the metrics
insight: Residue: an amino acid at a position. WT: reference sequence. OOF: out-of-fold predictions.
notes: Residue means an amino acid at a specific position; WT is the reference sequence. OOF predictions come from the fold in which that peptide or protein group was held out. MAE, AUROC/AP and top-k precision address different objectives and may use different eligible peptide populations.

title: Label construction and quality-control details
insight: Synonymous constructs provide intrinsic WT references; missing cells are masked and conditions kept separate.
notes: Use the WT reference appropriate to the assay. Synonymous constructs provide intrinsic WT estimates for saturation. Missing cells are masked rather than labelled zero. Source, condition, replicate and QC information remain attached to derived labels.

title: Reliability depends on the level of analysis
insight: Cohorts and position/cell definitions differ; this is not a paired comparison.
notes: Scanning ΔPSI Pearson correlation is 0.7229; saturation is 0.8335. Scanning Jaccard is position-based whereas saturation Jaccard is cell-based. Cohorts and denominators differ, so this is a description of reliability rather than a paired source comparison. Residual-noise and total-variance noise fractions are not interchangeable.

title: Composition models cannot distinguish every position
insight: Within a peptide, a composition-only model assigns the same score to the same substitution type.
notes: The invariance applies to composition-only models within the same peptide and for the same substitution type. It does not apply to all of PAP, which has a C-terminal channel, or to models using local context. The baseline named composition in the source also contains WT and mutant one-hot features. An oracle reading test labels describes representation limits, not model test performance.

title: Learning curves must distinguish individual models from ensembles
insight: Clustering sensitivity is a separate check; identical partitions are not additional evidence.
notes: The curve reports mean single-seed MAE. At fractions below 100%, different seeds use different training subsets; their ensemble may therefore see a larger union of examples than each member. Read single-fit data sensitivity from the individual-seed summary. Clustering sensitivity is separate, and repeated identical partitions are not additional independent evidence.

title: The tested interaction designs did not consistently beat the baseline
insight: These results concern the tested designs, not all possible nonlinear interactions.
notes: These interaction designs were tested on the restricted 91-peptide evaluation. The baseline and each candidate must be compared under the stated training conditions. The gate effect changes sign across seeds, and the tested FiLM/bilinear variants did not consistently improve over Ridge. This does not rule out all nonlinear interactions or future designs.

title: Removing duplicate cells does not remove peptide-level overlap
insight: Evaluate on held-out peptides or protein groups.
notes: The published Degformer checkpoint has 42,163 of 47,847 mutation cells in its training data, and all 91 WT peptides have been seen. Filtering exact mutant overlap leaves other mutations from the same peptides. Group-based retraining is needed for an unseen-peptide generalization claim. The figure uses the group-clean comparison and its corresponding baselines.

title: ESM scale comparisons belong to a separate evaluation design
insight: Do not directly compare these AUROCs with the full-range benchmark.
notes: This table describes ESM-augmented Ridge models on the 91-peptide design, not the full-range population. None of the size comparisons established a benefit under its stated criterion. Many checkpoint entries in a registry do not mean all have been evaluated. The full-range output currently evaluates only ESM2-35M.

title: Inspect several metrics for the same candidates
insight: Scores use mean predictions from three seeds and remain development analysis.
notes: The interactive appendix switches among MAE, positive AUROC and positive AP without changing model candidates or numerical values. All scores are computed from mean per-cell predictions of seeds 17, 29 and 43. The table remains development evidence rather than an unbiased estimate after model selection. For printing, a static MAE/AUROC figure is provided.

title: Scanning transfer: assess observed and remaining substitution types
insight: The 20-type cohort has 6,433 cells; the 360-type cohort has 115,979 cells. Both cover 235 peptides.
notes: For each peptide, only cells in the cohort being evaluated are included. The 20-type cohort has 114 peptides eligible for positive AUROC, versus 184 for the remaining 360 types. Do not directly compare those macro AUROCs as though the populations were identical. The plotted MAE intervals are descriptive posthoc intervals from 5,000 protein-group bootstrap resamples.

title: ClinVar supports region-level motivation, not residue-level validation
insight: ClinVar provides context and annotation, not ΔPSI ground truth.
notes: The protein-stratified Mantel–Haenszel odds ratio is about 2.14783, with 95% interval 2.07193–2.22651 over 3,114 informative strata. This is a region-level association, not causality. The exact-substitution saturation analysis has few classified variants, and its AUC interval still includes 0.5. ClinVar is not used as the model-selection target for ΔPSI.

title: E3 labels are too sparse for an E3-conditioned task
insight: Only one group has at least five peptides; menu choices are not learnable class counts.
notes: The E3/adaptor audit found only one group with at least five peptides. KLHL15 has 13 peptides, BAG6 has four, ASB7 and FEM1B have two each, and most remaining groups have one. The number of reported E3s or menu options is not evidence of enough examples to learn E3-conditioned specificity.

title: External sources need endpoint and usability audits
insight: Auditing a source does not establish external validation of the current model.
notes: Koren has not provided a completed model evaluation here; its scale and peptide length differ and it adds only five new groups, so it was not included in training. Larsen supplies tile scores rather than complete mutation ΔPSI labels. MaveDB structure analyses are exploratory, with endpoint and dimer issues still requiring review. SaProt true-3Di has no completed output; weights do not replace structure mapping.

title: Calibration and domain assessment answer different questions
insight: Reassess both when the model or data scope changes.
notes: Calibration asks whether predicted event probabilities match observed frequencies. Domain assessment asks whether the input resembles the conditions covered by the model and data. The two questions are different, and both require reassessment after changing models or scope. The displayed calibration evidence belongs to the tested Ridge model.

title: Reproducibility connects data, models and served results
insight: The manifest verified 2,986 files; baseline app tests do not validate new features.
notes: Checksums and sizes were verified for 2,986 snapshot files, including 83 OOF files across 47 recipes. Recomputed analysis matches the stored numbers. Baseline app tests in the documentation are historical evidence, not a new test run during slide creation. Results from a different local runtime must not be silently merged into the Kaggle campaign.

title: References and evidence are organized by topic
insight: Open Notes for the current slide's sources and interpretation limits.
notes: Sources are kept in Notes, the appendix, slide-sources.json and evidence.json instead of per-slide footnotes. The template/style websites informed the visual design, not model-performance claims. Asset notices identify the protein GIF, fonts and Chart.js.
